issues.legal_issue: Several shops selling grain on one plot constitute a market under a by-law that defines a market by reference to the number of shops.
material_facts: More than four shops stood on the land and compound owned by the accused.
The by-law treated a place with more than four shops on a plot as a market.
issues.conclusion: The shops constituted a market within the meaning of the by-law, and the by-law required the person controlling the land to obtain a licence.
issues.legal_principle: In the absence of a statutory definition, “market” in section 298(2)(F)(d) of the United Provinces Municipalities Act, 1916, may be read in its ordinary dictionary sense. Several shops selling grain on one plot fall within that sense and within the by-law’s definition.

predicates.multiple_shops_on_one_plot: More than one shop is kept on a single plot of land.
predicates.shops_sell_goods: The shops on the plot sell goods.
predicates.bylaw_defines_market_by_multiple_shops: The applicable by-law defines a market to include a place with multiple shops on one plot.

issues.definition: When multiple shops on one plot sell goods and the by-law defines such a place as a market, the place qualifies as a market.

issues.legal_issue: A provision regulating specified kinds of markets does not make that provision the exclusive source of authority to regulate markets, and it does not cover a market selling only grain.
material_facts: The market in question sold grain, and the courts below found that the shops sold no fruit, vegetables, fish, or meat.
The provision at issue applied to specified markets, including markets for fruit or vegetables and places used for selling certain animals or animal products.
The challenged by-law was also supported by the municipality’s market-regulation powers.
issues.conclusion: The provision did not apply to this grain market, and it did not invalidate an otherwise valid by-law regulating markets.
issues.legal_principle: Section 241(1) of the United Provinces Municipalities Act, 1916, does not include a market for the sale of grain alone. Nor does its reference to by-laws under heading F of section 298 make those by-laws the only permissible regulation: the word “only” cannot be read into the provision, and other by-laws may be made if otherwise valid under section 298.

predicates.market_sells_only_grain: The market sells grain and does not sell the other categories of goods specified in the relevant market-rights provision.
predicates.independent_market_rulemaking_authority: The municipality has a separate statutory basis for making rules regulating the market.

issues.definition: A grain-only market subject to an independent market-regulation power is not made exempt from valid regulation by the provision governing specified kinds of markets.

issues.legal_issue: A municipality may regulate and license markets under its specific powers concerning markets and its general power to further municipal administration.
material_facts: The municipality made by-laws requiring licences for markets and setting out licensing procedures and conditions.
More than four shops on the land sold grain.
The by-laws also provided for inspection and regulation of markets and related matters.
issues.conclusion: The challenged licensing and related by-laws were within the municipality’s authority and were valid.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 298(2)(F)(d) and (dd) of the United Provinces Municipalities Act, 1916, empower a municipality to make by-laws for the establishment, regulation, and inspection of markets and to prescribe licensing conditions and fees. The specific examples in section 298(2) are illustrative, not restrictive of the general power in section 298(1) to make by-laws for the furtherance of municipal administration. The Court relied on Emperor v. Sibnath Banerji & Ors., A.I.R. 1945 P.C. 156.

rule.if: municipal_bylaw_validity_challenge and multiple_grain_shops and bylaw_regulates_markets and bylaw_advances_municipal_administration

predicates.municipal_bylaw_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a municipality’s by-law.
predicates.multiple_grain_shops: Multiple shops on the same plot sell grain.
predicates.bylaw_regulates_markets: The municipality’s by-law provides for the establishment, regulation, inspection, or licensing of markets.
predicates.bylaw_advances_municipal_administration: The by-law is directed to furthering municipal administration.

issues.definition: In a challenge to a municipal by-law, a market-regulating by-law covering multiple grain shops and furthering municipal administration is within municipal authority.

issues.legal_issue: An inaccurate statement in a by-law’s preamble about the source of authority does not invalidate the by-law when the authority exists elsewhere.
material_facts: The by-laws’ preamble cited statutory clauses that did not apply.
The municipality nevertheless had power under other provisions to make the challenged by-laws.
issues.conclusion: The incorrect citation of authority in the preamble did not affect the validity of the by-laws.
issues.legal_principle: The validity of a by-law is tested by whether the body had power to make it, not by whether its preamble accurately identifies the source of that power. The Court relied on P. Balakotaiah v. Union of India & Ors., [1958] S.C.R. 1052.

predicates.bylaw_has_independent_authority: The body that made the by-law possessed authority under a provision other than the one cited in the preamble.
predicates.preamble_cites_inapplicable_power: The by-law’s preamble identifies a source of authority that does not apply.

issues.definition: A by-law remains valid when its maker had authority to enact it, even if its preamble cites an inapplicable source of power.

issues.legal_issue: A plea of mala fides that was not raised and supported by evidence at trial cannot be introduced for the first time on appeal.
material_facts: The accused argued at the appellate stage that the by-law had been made out of spite and enmity.
No appropriate allegations of mala fides had been made at trial, and no evidence had been led there to prove the plea.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not permit the plea of mala fides to be raised for the first time on appeal.
issues.legal_principle: A party alleging mala fides must make appropriate allegations at trial and lead evidence to prove them; the plea cannot be raised for the first time on appeal.

predicates.appeal_after_trial: The claim is made in an appeal following a trial.
predicates.malafides_claim_first_raised_on_appeal: A party first alleges at the appellate stage that an act was done out of spite or improper motive.
predicates.no_trial_allegations_or_evidence: The party made no appropriate trial allegations and led no trial evidence to establish the alleged improper motive.

issues.definition: In an appeal after trial, a claim of improper motive is not permitted when it is first raised on appeal and was neither alleged nor supported by evidence at trial.

issues.legal_issue: An abstract challenge to a fee that has not been imposed and whose amount depends on services rendered cannot be considered for the first time on appeal.
material_facts: The by-law authorized a fee up to a stated maximum, with the amount depending on the services rendered by the municipality.
No fee had been imposed on the accused.
The reasonableness challenge had not been raised in the courts below.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not consider the challenge to the fee because it had not been raised below and was premature in the absence of an imposed fee.
issues.legal_principle: A challenge to the reasonableness of a fee is premature when no fee has yet been imposed and its amount depends on the services actually rendered; a point not raised in the courts below cannot be considered in that abstract setting.

rule.if: appellate_fee_challenge and challenge_not_raised_below and no_fee_imposed and fee_depends_on_services

predicates.appellate_fee_challenge: A party challenges a fee provision in an appeal.
predicates.challenge_not_raised_below: The party did not raise the challenge in the lower courts.
predicates.no_fee_imposed: No fee has yet been charged to the party.
predicates.fee_depends_on_services: The amount of the fee depends on the services rendered by the public body.

issues.definition: An appellate challenge to a fee is not considered when it was not raised below, no fee has been imposed, and the amount depends on services rendered.

issues.legal_issue: Factual objections to a by-law’s publication or adoption procedure cannot be raised for the first time at the appellate stage when they should have been raised at trial.
material_facts: The accused sought to raise objections that the by-laws had not been published in the local paper and had not been made by special resolution.
Those objections were factual and had not been raised at trial.
The objections were sought to be introduced in the High Court appeal.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in refusing to allow the objections to be raised for the first time at the appellate stage.
issues.legal_principle: Factual pleas concerning procedural requirements for making by-laws should be raised at trial; they cannot be introduced for the first time on appeal. The objections concerned the publication requirement in section 94(3) and the special-resolution requirement in section 298(1) of the United Provinces Municipalities Act, 1916.

predicates.appellate_review_after_trial: The objection is made in an appeal following a trial.
predicates.procedural_objection_is_factual: The objection depends on facts about whether a required procedure was followed.
predicates.objection_first_raised_on_appeal: The party did not raise the objection at trial and first seeks to raise it on appeal.

issues.definition: A factual objection about compliance with a required procedure is not permitted when it is first raised on appeal after trial.
